title: What do you do when AI does not implement your instructions?
author: BJGG69
selftext:
I've been vibe-coding a few simple games and AI really struggles with the concept of spacing in particular. When asking for things to be larger/smaller, either nothing changes, or the whole composition gets out of proportion. 

Also, with 3D objects I constantly face the problem of clipping, with assets either going through each other, or colliding without contact. That's especially frustrating in racing games, where the objects come to a complete halt after a slightest hint of touching the racetrack outline.   
  
Many other smaller instances were I put in an instruction and it gets completely ignored. If you had other cases where you've been able to overcome the shortcomings of the AI builds, please also share.

comments.author: kkwikmick
comments.body: i usually swear at it and then remember that they may take over the world soon and remember it so i apologise

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
Sometimes you just gotta ask it where in the code that is controlled and fiddle with the variables urself. It’s usually a number, u can just tweak. Or you can give it a number specifically you want it to use. 

Those description words like larger or smaller is confusing to it cuz larger can mean a whole bunch of different sizes. It could be larger and u just not notice cuz it made such a small increase in size which is technically larger.

Vibe coding is alot easier if you ask it to explain the code and where something is controlled and why it did what it did.

comments.author: IcyBother8850
comments.body: Make the AI document and explain how your pathing, collision detection, spacing work in your game. Then use his explanations to more precisely guide him what you want changed. Also keep these documents inside the project it will help him reference it in the future

comments.author: manodrizzle
comments.body: If it's something visual, you can draw a mockup, or take a a screenshot and draw what/where it's supposed to look like and upload that with the next prompt.

comments.author: Nasilbitatbirakti
comments.body: Narrow down the issue. Clipping but why? Most of the time you need to figure out the root issue yourself then describe the solution to AI then it can turn into a script or whatever.

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body: I don't know why, have you had a case of clipping where you were able to get to the root cause?

replies.author: Nasilbitatbirakti
replies.body: I have no experience with 3D but for 2D in Godot the most common cause for clipping and collisions not working properly is either scaling the collisionshapes or not layering them up properly. You should be able to debug it tho. Take screenshots with collisionshapes visible and ask AI why it's not working.

comments.author: Low-Cook-3544
comments.body:
coming from someone who literally works for a vibe coding platform and makes games as part of their job:  
  
1. try reverse engineer it  
2. gaslight it

on 1: literally prompt "im seeing no changes from my perspective and i want to instruct you better. how would it be helpful for me to debug this? asset coordinates? reference sizes? what is the most efficient way to explain my ask?

on 2: this one works like a charm for me whenever AI attempts to do something i ask for and fails repeatedly but thinks it did the job. i say "you are clearly using an overcomplicated approach that is prone to errors and i'm not seeing any changes. try again but this time use a different, simplistic approach"

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body: I have a clear instruction that a task is not complete until it has been through a human play test. Everything the AI says it has done is supporting evidence but at the top of the tree are my eyeballs. It catches out some over confident agents and prevents the fix from being deleting, or patching the hell out of a problem.

replies.author: BJGG69
replies.body: That last prompt worked like a charm indeed

comments.author: Nice_Try4389
comments.body:
Stop vibe code do agentic coding with clear expectations, rules, measures, and auto coded tests.  Also use screenshots.  If something is off or I need something changed I take a screen shot, choose a reference point in that shot to have it compute movement and spacing against and give it the specific instruction of where mathematically I want it placed.  For example if I have an icon I want placed in the center of the panel I specifically tell it “find the center of X icon, place that center at the center of X panel, code so that icon stays in that position relative to the panel”, or for like scaling I will the it specifically what to scale and what to leave alone.  For example I had an icon with some text in it.  I liked the text size but it cut into the icon edges, and it was part of a series of the same icons in a row with different identifiers in them. I fed it a screenshot of that icon with the text problem, and told it specifically “there is currently an issue with this icon and the text cutting into the bounds of the icon, increase the scale of this and all of the same icon within this panel so that the text appropriately fits, do not increase the size of the contents of said icons”.

For the collisions make sure it is coding in bounding boxes and/or collision meshes to each object and coding so that when the code sees the intersection of bounding boxes or collision meshes is stops the objects from continuing further on that path or gives some kind of reflection of the collision.   Really pick up and skim some old game design books.  What you really need to do is learn how games work under the hood, not the code, but the actual tools games use to do what they do.   Once you understand that it is incredibly easy to get AI to do what you want as then you know what to ask it to actually implement.

But really just stop vibe coding and expecting it to just make a game and instead be very specific with what you are asking for.  Hell you can even open two sessions, tell the ne what you want to create, tell it you want to do it in a formal agentic process and ask it to provide you the prompts after making sure to ask you any clarifying questions it has on rules, mechanics and physics, and it will walk you step by step through setting up the project in the other session and giving you each prompt to copy and paste (tell it to put all prompts in a code box for one button copy and paste and you can do it from the your phone).  Will it give you a playable game overnight?  Nope it will take a couple of days but the code will be solid, you will largely just be copying and pasting prompts and you’ll have all the artifacts you need from architecture docs to code maps to traceability matrixs should you ever need to see how things work yourself or want to learn how it does what it does.

replies.author: Brewgazer
replies.body: I’m joking but tbh there’s a lot of us right now who have figured out great workflows to create games and it’s sorta turning into one of those I have this knowledge but idk how much of it to give out to people. If I was going to give you a tiny secret of my workflow it would be this. Understand what skills and rules do for your agent, and give your agent as many skills you can find that would help your project. Find skills for level design and game development, find skills for modeling cars in blender, find skills for modeling in blender in general. What it sounds like is you objects don’t have collision and are no clipping into each other.
